title: The General Theory of Verbal Humor
venue: The Routledge Handbook of Language and Humor (Routledge)
finding: Attardo's handbook chapter presents the GTVH as an expansion of Raskin's SSTH and situates it within his taxonomy of textual relationships; the abstract calls SSTH and GTVH the two most influential linguistic humour theories of recent decades.
why_for_us: Gives us the six-slot checklist (script opposition, logical mechanism, situation, target, narrative strategy, language) to annotate every 'Komputerka ktoś nakarmił?' variant before testing.

title: Toward an empirical verification of the General Theory of Verbal Humor
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Per authors, 534 participants rated similarity between anchor jokes and variants differing in only one of the six Knowledge Resources (script opposition, logical mechanism, situation, target, narrative strategy, language); the design tests whether perceived joke similarity follows the GTVH hierarchy of resources.
why_for_us: Model for our own testing: write minimal-pair versions of a gag that differ in one resource (e.g. only the target: notary vs. intern vs. client) and measure which change moves ratings most.

title: Script opposition and logical mechanism in punning
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Hempelmann applies the GTVH to imperfect puns, expanding and formalising the script opposition and logical mechanism knowledge resources to describe how near-homophone puns work.
why_for_us: Useful for Polish near-puns (e.g. 'komputerek' / 'kompotek'): the sound distance and the scripts both need to be strong enough to be noticed in 60-90 s.

title: Analyzing conversational data in GTVH terms: A new approach to the issue of identity construction via humor
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Archakis and Tsakona apply the GTVH to conversational narratives, combining it with sociopragmatic approaches; they treat script opposition as a necessary prerequisite and the laughter effect as a secondary criterion for labelling a narrative humorous, and link humour to identity and solidarity construction.
why_for_us: Our gags live inside office dialogue, so the GTVH should be applied to whole exchanges; the running gag can build in-group identity among office staff and viewers.

title: Humor norms for 4,997 English words
finding: Per authors, 821 crowdsourced participants each rated 211 words from 1 (humorless) to 5 (humorous), giving norms for 4,997 English words with reliability on a par with earlier norms; humour ratings were not well predicted by existing norms (valence, arousal, concreteness etc.).
why_for_us: Template for a small Polish word-humour norming run on our own vocabulary (notary jargon, diminutives like 'komputerek') before writing lines.

title: Wriggly, squiffy, lummox, and boobs: What makes some words funny?
finding: Using the Engelthaler & Hills norms, the authors predict word humour ratings (and ratings of previously unrated words) with reliability above the norms' own split-half reliability; per authors, words are judged funnier if less common and with improbable orthographic or phonological structure, and some semantic attributes fit superiority (scorn) theory.
why_for_us: Pick rarer, odd-sounding words for punch words (an archaic notarial term, an odd diminutive) rather than common ones.

title: Telling the world’s least funny jokes: On the quantification of humor as entropy
finding: Record has no abstract; per its keywords the study relates humour judgments of pseudowords (non-words) to Shannon entropy and word predictability.
why_for_us: Supports inventing low-probability letter strings for gibberish the AI 'komputerek' utters when hungry, but test them with listeners.

title: The linear organization of jokes: analysis of two thousand texts
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: No abstract in the record; per title and keywords (jokes, text structure) it is a corpus analysis of where the humorous element sits in about 2,000 joke texts, the basis of the claim that the punchline comes last.
why_for_us: Keep the disambiguating word of each gag ('nakarmił') at the very end of the line and of the episode beat.

title: Jab lines in narrative jokes
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: No abstract in the record; per title and keywords (punchline, narrative structure) Tsakona analyses jab lines, i.e. humorous lines placed inside the body of narrative jokes rather than at the end.
why_for_us: A 60-90 s episode can carry 2-3 jab lines before the final punchline; plan them so viewers are rewarded early (useful for swipe-away platforms).

title: An Analysis of the Course of a Joke's Telling in Conversation
venue: Explorations in the Ethnography of Speaking (Cambridge University Press)
finding: Sacks examines the sequential organisation of telling a dirty joke in conversation and finds its decisive feature is that the joke is built as a story, so it is told with the conversational machinery for stories.
why_for_us: A running gag works best when framed as a mini-story (who fed it, when) rather than a one-liner dropped into dialogue.

title: Laughter in Interaction
finding: Glenn's book synthesises 25 years of conversation-analytic research on the sequential organisation of laughter in everyday talk, showing that its production and placement relative to talk reveal its emergent meaning.
why_for_us: Where a character laughs (first or second, invited or not) carries meaning; script laughter placement deliberately instead of adding generic AI laughs.

title: Prosodic Markers of Saliency in Humorous Narratives
finding: Per authors' acoustic measurements, punch lines are not louder than the preceding text but have significantly lower pitch and slower speech rate, are not preceded by significant pauses, and are often (not always) marked by laughing or smiling voice; final position trumps saliency.
why_for_us: Direct TTS spec: deliver the punch line slower and lower, not louder, and do not insert a long dramatic pause before it.

title: The Prosodic Framing of Humour in Conversational Narratives: Evidence from Greek Data
finding: In 22 humorous conversational narratives with 170 jab lines (Praat analysis, 3 conversations of adolescent girls), per authors pauses around jab lines and differences in speech rate and intensity are systematically used to signal and delimit jab lines.
why_for_us: For jab lines (unlike final punch lines) a short pause and a change in rate/intensity is natural; small sample, so test with our voices.

title: Playful iconicity: structural markedness underlies the relation between funniness and iconicity
finding: Using collected and estimated ratings for over 70,000 English words, per authors funniness and iconicity ratings covary with cues of phonotactic complexity (structural markedness) that act as metacommunicative signals of playfulness; a distributional-semantics estimation method reproduces these correlations but amplifies biases in human ratings.
why_for_us: Marked, iconic-sounding forms (reduplication, odd clusters, onomatopoeia like 'chrup-chrup' when the komputerek 'eats') are a lexical lever for playfulness; LLM-estimated ratings inherit human bias.

title: Morphopragmatic View on the Ironic Use of Diminutives in Polish
finding: In a small informant-based study (12 respondents, 3 naturally occurring spoken sentences), per author Polish diminutives used ironically mostly drew a negative reaction, being perceived as an arrogant type of irony.
why_for_us: Key caution for 'komputerek': a diminutive aimed at a person can read as condescending; aim it at the machine (affectionate) and avoid diminutivising clients. Very small sample.

title: A preliminary typology of emotional connotations in morphological diminutives and augmentatives
finding: Across a sample of 19 languages, per author diminutives can express positive emotions (compassion, love, admiration) as well as contempt; diminutives are anchored in intimacy, while augmentatives relate more to broader social contexts.
why_for_us: Supports framing 'komputerek' as an intimacy marker (the office's pet machine); the same suffix can flip to contempt depending on target and tone.

title: 10 Challenges in analyzing Polish diminutives
venue: Diminutives across Languages, Theoretical Frameworks and Linguistic Domains (De Gruyter)
finding: Burkacka reviews Polish literature on diminutives: the most common suffix is -k- (-ka, -ko, -ek, -ik), suffixes can be stacked (first- and second-degree diminutives), and smallness couples with positive emotion and, for animal nouns, with youth/immaturity.
why_for_us: Second-degree forms ('komputereczek') give an escalation ladder for the running gag; the youth/animal coupling licenses treating the computer as a pet that must be fed.

title: Human-Centred Neural Reasoning for Subjective Content Processing Hate Speech, Emotions, and Humor
finding: A Wrocław team proposes personalised models that learn each annotator's Human Bias (HuBi); per authors, across 14 offensive, emotional and humour tasks the personalised methods radically outperformed generalised ones, and personalisation mattered more than choice of pretrained model.
why_for_us: Funniness labels are subjective; when we collect Polish ratings keep rater IDs and model per-rater bias rather than only averages.

title: A Computational Model of Linguistic Humor in Puns
finding: Kao, Levy and Goodman derive two information-theoretic measures (ambiguity and distinctiveness) from a sentence-processing model; per authors both correlate significantly with human funniness judgments of puns vs. regular sentences, and distinctiveness separates exceptionally funny puns from mediocre ones.
why_for_us: Checklist for Polish puns: both meanings must be supported (ambiguity) and each by different words in the line (distinctiveness); a pun where only the pun word carries the second meaning will be mediocre.

title: A processing fluency-account of funniness: Running gags and spoiling punchlines
finding: In four experiments, per author pre-exposing punchline words 15 min or even 1 min before a joke increased its funniness ratings, while pre-exposing them directly before the joke decreased funniness; pre-exposing the joke's beginning had no effect, and a font-fluency manipulation replicated the effect.
why_for_us: Direct support for the running gag: plant 'nakarmić/komputerek' earlier in the episode (or series) but not in the line right before the punch, so the payoff feels fluent rather than spoiled.

title: Sounds funny? Humor effects of phonological and prosodic figures of speech.
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts
finding: In a 2x2 design varying rhyme and meter in humorous couplets, per authors both rhyme and meter raised funniness ratings and sped processing; rhyming couplets also produced more intense, more positive affect, better comprehensibility and memory.
why_for_us: A rhymed or metrically 'mechanical' catchphrase (e.g. a doggerel the komputerek recites when hungry) should be funnier and more memorable than prose; cheap to A/B test.

title: Muting the Meaning A Social Function of Irony
finding: In two story-reading experiments, per authors ironic insults were rated less critical than literal ones (speaker seen as less annoyed, relationship less harmed), and ironic compliments less praising than literal ones, supporting the tinge hypothesis that irony mutes the literal evaluation.
why_for_us: Ironic barbs between notary and assistant keep the workplace warm; use irony when a character must criticise without becoming unlikeable.

title: Lower, Slower, Louder: Vocal Cues of Sarcasm
finding: No abstract in the record; the title states the reported vocal profile of (English) sarcasm: lower pitch, slower tempo and greater loudness, with keywords on listener perception.
why_for_us: First-pass prosody target for sarcastic lines in TTS, but see the French contrary profile and verify on Polish listeners.

title: Prosodic cues of sarcastic speech in French: slower, higher, wider
finding: In a corpus of French declarative utterances, per authors sarcastic productions show utterance lengthening, increased F0 modulation and globally raised pitch level and range.
why_for_us: Contradicts the 'lower' English profile: sarcasm prosody is language-specific, so do not copy English TTS settings to Polish without a listening test.

title: Recognizing sarcasm without language: A cross-linguistic study of English and Cantonese
finding: In a crossed design, per authors English and Cantonese listeners identified sarcasm from prosody in their native language but only at near-chance levels in the unfamiliar language, whereas other attitudes (sincerity, humorous irony, neutrality) were recognised relatively better across languages.
why_for_us: Sarcastic prosody requires native-language experience: AI voices for Polish must be judged by native Polish listeners, and an English-tuned voice may make sarcasm unreadable.

title: Context and Intonation in the Perception of Sarcasm
finding: 82 participants heard monotone stories with positive or negative context followed by a sarcastic or sincere statement; per authors a context x tone interaction meant incongruent context/tone produced mid-range sarcasm ratings and longer response times.
why_for_us: Sarcasm lands fastest when the scene context and the voice agree; if the TTS tone is off, viewers hesitate, which kills timing in 60-90 s.

title: Egocentrism over e-mail: Can we communicate as well as we think?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Across five experiments, per authors people overestimate how well they convey tone such as sarcasm or humour over e-mail without paralinguistic cues, an overconfidence attributed to egocentrism.
why_for_us: Writers (and LLMs) judging their own script on the page overrate its irony; test the voiced and subtitled version with naive viewers.

title: Sarcasm in Written Communication: Emoticons are Efficient Markers of Intention
finding: In two production studies, per authors tongue and wink emoticons were the principal markers of sarcastic intent in text, while ellipsis was associated more with criticism than sarcasm.
why_for_us: For on-screen captions and the komputerek's chat bubbles, a wink/tongue emoji can disambiguate sarcasm; avoid '...' if the line should read as playful.

title: Polski dowcip językowy
finding: Book record without abstract: Danuta Buttler's classic monograph on Polish linguistic wit (verbal humour mechanisms in Polish).
why_for_us: The standard Polish taxonomy of language-based jokes; consult it when classifying our wordplay on 'komputerek' / 'nakarmić'.

title: Niezgodność i jej rozwiązanie: O humorystycznych puentach z perspektywy językoznawczej
finding: Krasowska reviews linguistic accounts of incongruity and its resolution (IDM, SSTH, GTVH, FR) and tests them on 16th-century Polish jokes from Górnicki's Dworzanin polski; per author most assumptions are confirmed, but the idea of one general resolution mechanism is rejected.
why_for_us: A Polish-language bridge between GTVH and native joke material; suggests we need several resolution types, not one formula, when prompting LLMs for punchlines.

title: Cultural Wars in Polish Political Humor
venue: Political Humor Worldwide (Springer, The Language of Politics)
finding: Record has no abstract; per its keywords Brzozowska and Chłopicki discuss Polish political humour in the context of culture wars and polarisation, class, literary tradition, film and popular culture, irony, parody and intertextuality.
why_for_us: Polish humour is polarised along political lines; keep the notary-office gags apolitical to avoid losing half the audience.

title: Stereotypical Poles and Their Funny Beaver (Bober)
finding: Chłopicki and Brzozowska analyse the viral 'bober' video; they hypothesise its humour and spread came from the maker's exaggerated emotional reaction and his language (a recognisable Polish profanity), re-activating stereotypes of the emotional Pole, and track its spread into memes and songs across Slavdom.
why_for_us: A recent Polish case of a short-form running meme: exaggerated emotional reaction plus one iconic phrase is what travelled, a model for 'Komputerka ktoś nakarmił?'.

title: A cross-cultural study of humor appreciation: Italy and Germany
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Using Italian translations of the 3 WD humour test (funniness and aversiveness of incongruity-resolution, nonsense and sexual humour) with 148 Italian vs. 148 German adults, per authors the factor structure replicated across countries, while Italians rated sexual humour higher and nonsense humour lower than Germans.
why_for_us: The 3WD taxonomy and its two-scale rating (funny vs. aversive) transfer across European languages; a Polish adaptation could classify our lines and pre-screen raters' humour taste.

title: Zamierzona niepoprawność językowa jako źródło komizmu w serialu „Świat według Kiepskich”
finding: Maćkowiak documents intended language errors as a source of comedy in the Polish sitcom 'Świat według Kiepskich', noting hundreds of examples across 431 episodes up to 2013 and the writers' claim that the script used only really existing (often overheard) language elements.
why_for_us: Deliberate, overheard-sounding errors (e.g. a client mangling 'akt notarialny') are a proven Polish TV comedy device; use sparingly so the notary stays competent.

title: The carnival of the absurd: Stanislaw Bareja's alternatywy 4
venue: Popular Television in Eastern Europe (book chapter, BIROn Birkbeck repository)
finding: Chapter record without its own abstract (only the volume synopsis on socialist and postsocialist entertainment TV): Ostrowska discusses Bareja's TV series 'Alternatywy 4' as a carnival of the absurd.
why_for_us: Bareja's absurd-bureaucracy tradition is the obvious Polish reference frame for office humour; viewers will read our notary office against it.

title: BIUROKRACJA I BIUROKRACI W RADZIECKIEJ KOMEDII FILMOWEJ
finding: Cybulski surveys how Soviet film comedies from 1927 to 1988 depicted bureaucratic distortions and stigmatised bureaucratism, from Protazanov through Aleksandrov to Ryazanov and Gaidai.
why_for_us: Shows the long Central/Eastern European comic tradition of mocking officials; our notary must be the competent one surrounded by absurd procedure, not the butt. Small university journal.

title: Inside Jokes: Identifying Humorous Cartoon Captions
finding: Using crowdsourced judgments on thousands of New Yorker contest captions per cartoon, the authors build a corpus of funnier vs. less-funny caption pairs; per authors their classifier picks the funnier of two captions 69% of the time when both hinge on the same joke and 64% for any pair.
why_for_us: Pairwise 'which is funnier?' on variants of the same joke is the format that both humans and models handle best; build our Polish line tests as same-joke pairs.

title: Humor in Collective Discourse: Unsupervised Funniness Detection in the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest
finding: Comparing a dozen automatic methods for picking the funniest of 5,000+ reader captions per cartoon, per authors negative sentiment, human-centeredness and lexical centrality most strongly matched the funniest captions, followed by positive sentiment.
why_for_us: Lines centred on a person and a mild negative (the office is broke, the komputerek is starving) are favoured; 'central' wording that many writers converge on tends to win.

title: Humor in AI: Massive Scale Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Benchmarks for Cartoon Captioning
finding: Per authors the dataset holds over 250 million crowdsourced ratings on more than 2.2 million New Yorker captions over eight years; benchmarks using GPT-4 and human judgments show RLHF/DPO fine-tuning is limited for creative tasks and that GPT-4 and Claude underperform top human contestants at writing funny captions.
why_for_us: LLM drafts are a starting pool, not the final line: keep a human comedy pass and rank candidates with real viewer preferences.

title: Do Androids Laugh at Electric Sheep? Humor “Understanding” Benchmarks from The New Yorker Caption Contest
finding: Three tasks (matching a caption to a cartoon, identifying the winning caption, explaining why it is funny); per authors the best multimodal models trail humans by 30 accuracy points on matching, and human-written explanations beat few-shot GPT-4 explanations head-to-head in more than 2/3 of cases.
why_for_us: Do not let an LLM be the sole judge of whether a visual gag in a 9:16 frame works; humans still read image-text jokes far better.

title: SemEval-2020 Task 7: Assessing Humor in Edited News Headlines
finding: Shared task on crowd-rated edited headlines with two subtasks: regress funniness on a 0-3 scale and choose the funnier of two edited versions of the same headline; per authors it attracted 48 and 31 teams respectively, the most popular computational humour task to date.
why_for_us: Ready-made protocol for our tests: a 0-3 funniness scale plus pairwise choice between one-word edits of the same line.

title: “President Vows to Cut <Taxes> Hair”: Dataset and Analysis of Creative Text Editing for Humorous Headlines
finding: Humicroedit: 15,095 English headlines edited (usually one-word replacement) to be funny, each scored by five crowd judges; per authors the data support incongruity, superiority and setup/punchline theories, and baseline classifiers predict whether an edit is funny.
why_for_us: One-word substitution is a cheap, measurable way to generate gag variants ('Komputerka ktoś [nakarmił/podlał/wyprowadził]?') and rate them.

title: ChatGPT is fun, but it is not funny! Humor is still challenging Large Language Models
finding: In prompt-based experiments on generation, explanation and detection, per authors over 90% of 1,008 jokes generated by ChatGPT were the same 25 jokes; it explained valid jokes accurately but invented explanations for invalid ones, and joke-typical surface features misled its classification.
why_for_us: Expect LLM joke drafts to collapse onto a few stock patterns; force diversity (constraints, many seeds, dedupe) and never trust an LLM's explanation of why a line is funny.

title: How funny is ChatGPT? A comparison of human- and A.I.-produced jokes
finding: In two blind-rating studies, ChatGPT 3.5 and laypeople answered the same humour prompts, and ChatGPT wrote Onion-style headlines compared with published Onion headlines; per authors ChatGPT's jokes were rated equally funny or funnier than human ones regardless of task or writer expertise.
why_for_us: Contradicts 'LLMs are not funny': for short, prompt-bound jokes LLM output can match humans in blind ratings, so blind A/B tests (source hidden) are the fair way to choose lines.

title: Does Bigger Mean Funnier? Evaluating Humor Generation Across the Qwen3 Model Family
finding: Jokes from five Qwen3 variants (8B-235B) on 50 themes: per authors an automated LLM judge gave a perfect monotonic size-win-rate ranking while human annotators found no significant aggregate difference (largest model preferred only on themes where annotators agreed, p = 0.039); the LLM judge showed severe position and length biases.
why_for_us: LLM-as-judge will invent differences between our drafts; if used, randomise order, length-match candidates and calibrate against a Polish human panel.

title: Getting Serious about Humor: Crafting Humor Datasets with Unfunny Large Language Models
finding: Per authors current LLMs are good at 'unfunning' jokes (editing them into minimally different non-humorous texts), as judged by humans and by downstream humor detection; GPT-4 synthetic data in code-mixed English-Hindi was rated highly by bilingual annotators.
why_for_us: Use an LLM to create 'unfunny twins' of each Polish line as controls in our tests, which isolates the word that carries the joke.

title: Speech-laughs: An HMM-based approach for amused speech synthesis
finding: Trained on neutral speech, speech-smile and laughter, the authors synthesised speech-laughs either from neutral speech plus laughter bursts or from smiled speech plus laughter bursts; per authors listener ratings showed a compound effect of laughter bursts and smile on both perceived amusement and naturalness.
why_for_us: For an amused line, combine a smiled voice with short laughter bursts rather than a laugh glued onto neutral TTS; check whether our ElevenLabs v3+ voices expose such controls.

title: Auditory smiles trigger unconscious facial imitation
finding: Using a voice transformation that simulates the spectral signature of speaking with stretched lips, per authors listeners' zygomatic (smile) muscles tracked auditory smile gestures in spoken sentences even when listeners did not consciously detect the smile.
why_for_us: A 'smiling voice' setting can make viewers smile without noticing it; the effect is measurable with facial EMG or webcam coding in our tests.

title: Can Duchenne smiles be feigned? New evidence on felt and false smiles.
finding: Per authors similar amounts of Duchenne and non-Duchenne smiles occurred in spontaneous (amusing material) and posed conditions, and the Duchenne marker had limited predictive value compared with asymmetry, apex duration and non-positive facial actions, raising doubts about its validity as a sign of enjoyment.
why_for_us: If we use webcam facial coding to score funniness, do not equate a Duchenne smile with 'found it funny'; use dynamics (duration, onset) and pair with ratings.

title: Will the real relationship between facial expression and affective experience please stand up: The case of exhilaration
finding: Female participants in three alcohol conditions viewed 30 joke/cartoon slides; per author within-subject correlations between rated funniness and smiling/laughter were higher than between-subject ones, aggregation raised within-subject coefficients, and cheerful mood produced hyper-expressiveness (smiling at low funniness).
why_for_us: Compare a viewer's reactions across our gags (within-person), not viewers against each other; a cheerful panel will smile at weak lines.

title: The Effects of Audience Laughter on Men's and Women's Responses to Humor
finding: 40 participants heard a radio comedy with or without audience laughter while being covertly videotaped; per authors those with laughter present rated it funnier and more enjoyable and laughed more (smiling difference not significant), with no sex differences.
why_for_us: Laugh tracks inflate ratings: test our episodes with and without added laughter, and never compare a laugh-track version with a dry one.

title: Few-Shot Prompting, Full-Scale Confusion: Evaluating Large Language Models for Humor Detection in Croatian Tweets
finding: GPT-4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash labelled humour in 6,000 Croatian tweets against expert gold labels; per authors LLM-human agreement (kappa = 0.28) matched human-human agreement (kappa = 0.27), while LLM-LLM agreement was much higher (kappa = 0.63), so models behave like one more human annotator.
why_for_us: The closest evidence for a Slavic language: an LLM judge of Polish humour is roughly as (un)reliable as one human rater, and two LLMs agreeing with each other proves nothing; use them to pre-filter, not to decide.

title: Best-Worst Scaling More Reliable than Rating Scales: A Case Study on Sentiment Intensity Annotation
finding: In a direct comparison on sentiment intensity annotation, per authors best-worst scaling produced significantly more reliable results than a rating scale for the same total number of annotations.
why_for_us: For ranking 10-20 candidate punchlines, show viewers sets of 4 and ask 'funniest / least funny' instead of 1-5 Likert; evidence is from sentiment, not humour, so verify.

title: Comparative Judgments as an Alternative to Ratings: Identifying the Scale Origin.
finding: Böckenholt notes that comparative (pairwise) judgments cannot by themselves recover the scale origin: one item judged better than another says nothing about whether either is attractive; he presents nested-model methods to estimate the origin.
why_for_us: Pairwise A/B tests tell us which line is funnier, not whether any is funny; add one absolute anchor question (would you share this? 0-3 funny) to each test.

title: Rating norms should be calculated from cumulative link mixed effects models
finding: Per authors, means and SDs of Likert ratings distort distances between items because the data are ordinal; in simulations and a reanalysis of a rating-norms dataset, cumulative link mixed models normed items more accurately and separated item scores from participants' response biases.
why_for_us: Analyse our 1-5 funniness ratings with ordinal mixed models (rater and line as random effects), not raw averages, before declaring a winner.

title: Large Dataset and Language Model Fun-Tuning for Humor Recognition
finding: Per authors a Russian corpus of more than 300,000 jokes and funny dialogues paired with lexically similar unfunny texts was built (manual check of 2,000 items), and a fine-tuned language model reached F1 = 0.91 on humour recognition.
why_for_us: A Slavic precedent for building a Polish humour corpus with matched unfunny controls; note that recognising 'joke-shaped' text is not the same as predicting funniness.
